As I recall SCOPe (from pretrained knowledge, not checked against a release), these three sit together in class b (all-beta), fold b.6 (cupredoxin-like), superfamily b.6.1 (Cupredoxins). They are separate families within that superfamily. Plastocyanin/azurin-like proteins are family b.6.1.1. The ephrin ectodomain (the Eph receptor-binding domain of ephrins) and the PAD4 N-terminal domain are, as I remember it, separate families in the same superfamily. I am less sure of the exact family numbers for those two, so check them against the release in use. The shared feature is a Greek-key beta-sandwich core.

In SCOPe, 'same superfamily' means a probable common evolutionary origin. That is inferred from structure, and sometimes from functional features, even when sequence identity is low. It is a statement about distant homology of the fold. It is not a statement that function is conserved. The families are distinct, so there is no close-homology basis for transferring sequence-level annotation. The relationship is also much weaker than membership in one family.

Copper binding and electron transfer should not be inferred across them. In plastocyanin and azurin, the type-1 copper site is built from specific loop residues: two His, one Cys and usually a Met. Redox activity depends on this site. Ephrin ectodomains are receptor-binding, cell-surface signalling ligands. The PAD4 N-terminal domain is a regulatory or structural part of a calcium-dependent citrullinating enzyme. As far as I know, neither has the copper ligand set or an electron-transfer role. The shared scaffold has been adapted to quite different functions, so the fold gives no evidence of metal binding. Any claim about copper or redox activity needs direct evidence. That means conserved ligand residues in an alignment, a metal-bound structure, or biochemical or spectroscopic data. Even within b.6.1, function varies: cupredoxin-like domains also appear in multicopper oxidases and nitrite reductases, so the fold alone is not enough to assign function.
